title: Stand-In Station for Each Check
statement:
There are c power stations numbered 1 to c. Each pair [a, b] in connections is a two-way cable. Stations that can reach each other through cables form one grid. Cables never change.

All stations start online. Then the queries are processed in order:

  • [1, x]: a check request for station x. If x is online, it handles the check itself and the answer is x. Otherwise the answer is the smallest-numbered online station in the same grid as x, or -1 if every station in that grid is offline.
  • [2, x]: station x goes offline. It stays offline for good. An offline station still belongs to its grid: cables through it keep connecting the others.

Return the answers to the type-1 queries, in order.

examples.why: After 1 and 2 go offline, the only online station in grid {1, 2, 3} is 3. Once 3 is off too, that grid answers -1. Station 4 is online and answers for itself.
The stand-in is the smallest online id in the grid, not the nearest neighbour of 3.
Station 2 is alone in its grid, so once it is offline nobody can stand in. Switching it off twice changes nothing.

constraints: 1 ≤ a, b ≤ c, a ≠ b, no repeated cable
queries[i] = [type, x] with type ∈ {1, 2}, 1 ≤ x ≤ c
hints: The grids never change, only which stations are online. Can you work out the grids once, up front?
Union-find (or one BFS per grid) labels every station with its grid. Then each grid needs a structure that returns its smallest online id.

Stations only ever go offline. List each grid's ids in increasing order and keep a pointer to the first one that might still be online; skip offline ids by moving the pointer forward. Each id is skipped at most once.

explain.intuition:
Two separate jobs hide here. First, which grid is each station in? The cables are fixed, so union-find (or BFS) answers that once before any query. Second, what is the smallest online id in a grid? That set only shrinks, which makes it easy.

Give every grid its ids in sorted order and a pointer starting at the front. When asked, move the pointer past ids that are offline and report the first online one. The pointer never moves back, because an offline station never comes back online. Over all queries each id is skipped at most once, so the total work is linear. A min-heap with lazy deletion does the same job and also works if stations could return.
steps: Union every cable's two endpoints in a union-find over 1 … c.
Loop id = 1 … c and append id to the list of find(id). Each list ends up sorted for free.
Keep offline[id] and one pointer per grid, starting at 0.
Type 1: if x is online, answer x. Otherwise advance the grid's pointer while it points at an offline id; answer that id, or -1 if the pointer ran off the end.
pitfalls: Removing the offline station from the graph. It stays a link in the cables; in [[1, 2], [2, 3]] with 2 offline, 1 and 3 are still in one grid.
Answering with the smallest online id even when x itself is online. An online station handles its own check.
Running a BFS per query. With 200 000 queries on a big grid that is far too slow.

solutions.title: Search the grid on every check
solutions.idea: For each type-1 query on an offline station, BFS its grid and take the smallest online id.

solutions.title: Union-find + sorted list with a forward pointer
solutions.idea: Group ids by grid in increasing order. Because stations only go offline, each grid's smallest online id is found by a pointer that only moves forward.

followups: Stations can also come back online. What replaces the forward pointer? (A min-heap with lazy deletion, or a sorted set.)
Cables can be cut over time too. Why does processing the queries in reverse help?
